spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment evaluated whether TransformerEngine NCCL_EP could replace or beat Marin's incumbent `a2a_cute` expert-parallel MoE path on GB200/B200 systems. The core goal was met: TE/NCCL_EP builds, imports, and trains at 64 GPUs with EP8, with loss parity and near-parity throughput. A custom NCCL_EP transport seam plus MoE-layer chunking made the production b1024 x seq4096 d5120 L48 case train at 18.0% MFU versus 19.1% for `a2a_cute`, and chunk rematerialization removed the no-drop EP capacity wall by making peak EP memory scale with one chunk rather than full batch/seqlen. The later fairness and gap-closing work found that TE's full `moe()` block performs about the same as the custom seam but remains around 1.1-1.3 percentage points behind `a2a_cute`; command-buffer scoping, collective-overlap flags, and `max_num_sms` tuning were wash-or-loss in bf16. The current recommendation is to keep `a2a_cute` as the incumbent for bf16, preserve NCCL_EP/chunking as a derisked path, and next pursue NVIDIA/TE follow-ups: report the TE main-tip 64-GPU regression, test quantized fp8/MXFP8 support when available, and revisit NGC-stack arms after the compile stall is understood.

### Helpful links
- Full logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md
- 64-GPU EP8 goal gate: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7331#issuecomment-5008121573
- Production b1024 chunking result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7331#issuecomment-5009585521
- Full TE MoE block benchmark: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7331#issuecomment-5073227834
- Gap-closing benchmark and TE tip regression: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7331#issuecomment-5076118699
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

NVIDIA's recommendations for EP MoE on JAX/XLA GPU (2026-07-13/14):

1. `jax.ragged_dot` was made performant in NGC JAX 26.05 (`xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_fusion=ON`, confirmed supported on B200).
2. TransformerEngine has a MoE block backed by NCCL_EP ([TE #3036](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/pull/3036), C API in [TE #3034](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/pull/3034)) — "equivalent to DeepEP/HybridEP with no external dependency". The 8k-seq-len staging limit (which caps local batch size at 2) is actively being removed.
3. The JAX MoE speed-of-light solution will require TransformerEngine as the time-to-market way to expose NCCL_EP.

The full TE MoE block (router/permute, hybridEP A2A, grouped GEMMs) lives on the WIP branch [`jberchtold/teddy-te-ep-integration-2026-07-08-support-quantization`](https://github.com/jberchtold-nvidia/TransformerEngine/blob/jberchtold/teddy-te-ep-integration-2026-07-08-support-quantization/transformer_engine/jax/moe.py), targeted for merge into TE main. Early external testing of that branch is reportedly promising.

Prior state on our side (#7012 / #7279): hypothesis H-te is Blocked in the [7012 logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md) — a 2026-07-15 API probe found TE 2.15.0+42b840051 ships `grouped_dense`/`permutation`/`router` but no NCCL_EP JAX surface. A source read of the TE PRs noted: 8192-token `max_tokens_per_rank` staging default, bf16-only dispatch wire (fp8 wire on the quantization WIP branch), one-sided `max_num_sms`, process-per-GPU requirement, and that it disables NCCL comm-splitting and command-buffer capture. #7279's hypothesis queue already ranks the NCCL_EP-style chunked-pipeline decomposition #1 by expected value.

## Hypothesis or Goal

NCCL_EP's SM-capped persistent comm kernels feeding chunked expert GEMMs beat our current EP legs in the latency-bound NVL72 regime. Concretely:

1. Build TE from the WIP branch on the B200 container stack and get the JAX MoE block importable.
2. Microbench dispatch/combine vs our measured baselines: XLA `ragged_all_to_all` one-shot kernel pathology (~297 ms/call, B200MFU-018) and the NCCL fallback (one-shot kernel disabled, B200MFU-025).
3. If the microbench wins, e2e MFU comparison at the canonical d2560 MoE config vs the current best (ring_cute EP4, 20.83% at 64 GPUs, #7279).
4. Assess the fp8/MXFP8 dispatch-wire path as the follow-on (dispatch bytes halve; ties into the MXFP8 work in #7282).

Caveat from prior evidence: SM-capping alone was falsified twice on this stack (B200MFU-016, B200MFU-021) — the value, if any, is in the chunked-pipeline decomposition and the fused dispatch, not the SM budget.

## Status

Goal met for build/import/train and production-shape derisking. NCCL_EP is not currently recommended as the bf16 default over `a2a_cute`: the best TE-backed arms remain about 1.3 percentage points behind `a2a_cute`, and the latest TE main tip regresses at the full 64-GPU data8 x expert8 topology. Next steps are NVIDIA escalation for that regression, quantized fp8/MXFP8 wire when TE exposes it, and NGC-stack retests after the compile stall is understood.

## Links

* Logbook: [.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md) (branch `research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep`)
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: prior context in #7012 (H-te) and #7279 (hypothesis queue)

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-001 (source read): the dependency chain is **fully public** — no closed libnccl_ep artifact.

- TE PRs #3034 (C API + NCCL EP backend) and #3036 (JAX `ep_dispatch`/`ep_combine` primitives + VJPs) are **merged into TE main** (June 13/27); the WIP branch is only needed later for the fp8 dispatch wire. The negative 2026-07-15 probe is explained: that wheel predates the JAX merge.
- `libnccl_ep.a` builds from the in-tree `3rdparty/nccl` submodule pinned to public NVIDIA/nccl `b87848fbc` (v2.30u1 line) and links statically; `NVTE_WITH_NCCL_EP=ON` is the TE build default.
- Runtime gate: system NCCL >= 2.30.4 (our stack runs 2.28.9; PyPI `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` has aarch64 wheels).
- Contract at the merged surface: process-per-GPU (`local_device_count()==1`), bf16-only wire, TE MeshResource ep axis, num_experts % ep_size == 0. Staging math at the reference config (65,536 tokens/rank): zero-drop recv capacity at EP8 is ~21.4 GiB/rank — sizing to expected load × margin is one of the at-scale questions this issue exists to answer.

Next: build TE main (tip `68493d2d`) inside the NGC container on a GB200 node, import-probe the `te.jax.ep` surface (NCCLEP-002). Details in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-002: **TE + NCCL_EP builds and imports on the goal platform.**

Wheel `transformer_engine-2.18.0.dev0+68493d2` (TE main, sm_100a, arm64) built natively on a GB200 iris pod with a synthetic CUDA_HOME assembled from pip cu13 wheels — no container. Import probe under **stock jax 0.10.1** on 4×GB200 shows the full `te.jax.ep` surface (`ep_bootstrap`/`ep_dispatch`/`ep_combine`); runtime NCCL upgraded to 2.30.7 (EP gate is >= 2.30.4). Wheel is stashed in object storage; build recipe is `experiments/ncclep/build_te_wheel.sh` on the research branch (11 attempts; the gotcha list is in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md)).

One design constraint surfaced by source read: TE EP supports a **single** dp/fsdp axis outside `ep`, so the replica-2 × 32-GPU-copy reference layout won't bootstrap as-is — the first 64-GPU EP8 target will be a single-copy data8×expert8 mesh (still ≥32-way sharded); replica-DP-outside is worth reporting upstream.

In flight: single-node 4-proc TE EP test-suite smoke, then EP4 / cross-node EP8 transport microbenches.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-003: **NCCL_EP is running on our stack** — TE's full multi-process EP test suite passes (13/13 in 17.7 s) on 4×GB200, one process per GPU: bootstrap, dispatch/combine primitive round trips, custom_vjp gradient closed-form checks, and the HLO guard that no XLA collectives leak around the EP FFI ops.

Two runtime discoveries on the way (fixes in `experiments/ncclep/` on the research branch):
- The gpu venv's cu12 wheels (torch deps) leaked into the first build's link (`libcublas.so.12` soname mismatch) — the toolchain merge is now cu13-only and the smoke asserts TE core's DT_NEEDED is clean.
- **NCCL_EP JIT-compiles its device kernels at bootstrap** via an external nvcc: every rank needs nvcc + CUDA headers + the generated `nccl_ep` JIT header tree at runtime (none packaged in the wheel). The build job now stashes the headers; launchers set `NCCL_EP_JIT_*` env.

In flight: transport microbenches at reference shapes (65,536 tokens/rank × hidden 5120 × top-4) — EP4 single-node and EP8 across 2 nodes (first cross-node NCCL_EP over MNNVL). Details in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-005: **NCCL_EP trains end-to-end in the standalone MFU bench with loss parity.**

New `--moe-implementation nccl_ep` backend on branch `mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep-ncclep`: TE `ep_dispatch` → shard_map(QuACK grouped FFN via the `expert_mlp_fn` seam) → weighted hadamard → TE `ep_combine`, mirroring TE's own MoE block. Single-node EP4 smoke (d2560 L4 b16, process-per-GPU) vs a ring_cute control at the identical config: **step-0 loss bit-identical** (11.805191040039062), full 6-step trajectory parity to ~2e-5.

Notable integration findings (details in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md)):
- Command-buffer capture must be off around the EP FFI ops (TE's pointer-keyed handle cache), with `NVTE_EP_HANDLE_CACHE_SIZE=-1` — TE's own documented JAX workaround.
- **NCCL_EP has no drop path**: recv overflow is an OOB write that poisons the CUDA context, so capacity must be provisioned for the no-drop worst case (`ep × tokens × top_k` ≈ 21.5 GiB/rank at the reference config) — sub-worst-case capacity needs TE-side drop support (worth an upstream ask).
- The capacity tail of the dispatch buffer is uninitialized; grouped-GEMM wgrads over garbage rows NaN'd training until the tail was zeroed + the combine weighting switched from 0-mask multiply to `where`.
- TE's sharding rules assume auto-sharding meshes — the EP region runs under `jax.sharding.auto_axes` inside our explicit-sharding bench.

In flight (NCCLEP-006, the goal gate): 64-GPU **EP8** at the reference config (d5120 L48 e64 top4 b1024 seq4096; single-copy data8×expert8 per TE's single-outer-axis constraint) + an a2a_cute EP8 control at the identical mesh and flags.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-006: **Goal met — NCCL_EP trains at 64 GPUs with EP8 at a production-shape config, at parity loss and near-parity MFU with the incumbent EP backend.**

All arms: d5120 L48 e64 top4 seq4096, EP8, single 64-GPU model copy (data8×expert8; TE's single-outer-axis constraint), 16-node GB200 gang, one process per GPU, EP groups spanning 2 nodes over MNNVL, recompute_all, 20 steps.

| arm | batch | steady MFU (B200 conv.) | s/step | tok/s | final loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a2a_cute EP8 (baseline) | 1024 | 19.1 % | 15.7 | 266 k | 8.746 |
| a2a_cute EP8 (control) | 512 | 18.1 % | 8.3 | 252 k | 8.762 |
| **nccl_ep EP8** (first pass) | 512 | 7.3 % | 20.4 | 103 k | **8.760** |
| **nccl_ep EP8** (+tail fix) | 512 | **16.7–17.1 %** | 8.9 | 233–240 k | **8.760** |

The tail fix: the QuACK expert-GEMM seam extended the last expert group across the entire no-drop capacity buffer, multiplying FFN work ~4× — skipping the extension (safe once real rows are `where`-selected before combine) recovered 7.3 % → ~17 %. The remaining ~1 pp gap to a2a_cute is untuned: command buffers are globally disabled (required around EP FFI ops; could be scoped), a redundant tail-zeroing pass remains, and `max_num_sms` is at auto.

Scale-derisk findings (the point of this issue):

1. **b1024 at EP8 does not fit**: NCCL_EP has no drop path, so recv capacity must cover the worst case, and worst-case capacity scales ∝ `EP degree × per-rank tokens`. At b1024/EP8 that is 2.1 M rows/rank → a 172 GiB temp arena → OOM. This is NVIDIA's "8k max_tokens_per_rank limits local batch to 2" wall seen from the other side — their intended shape is small per-dispatch chunks. Upstream asks: capacity-clipped dispatch with drop accounting, or the chunked-dispatch mode; on our side, MoE-layer chunking would unlock big batches.
2. **Cross-node EP works out of the box** on the NVL72 rack (EP groups span nodes over MNNVL; NCCL_EP treats the whole rack as one NVLink domain).
3. Every rank needs the **JIT toolchain at runtime** (nvcc + CUDA headers + the generated `nccl_ep` header tree) — NCCL_EP JIT-compiles its device kernels at first use; a disk cache makes this a one-time ~2 min cost per config.
4. TE EP supports **one dp/fsdp axis outside `ep`** — replica-DP outside an FSDP×EP copy (our reference layout) won't bootstrap; worth an upstream request.

Reproduction: branch `mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep-ncclep` (backend + bench wiring + launchers), wheel build recipe on `research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep` (`experiments/ncclep/`), full narrative in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md). Jobs: `/mwittmann/ncclep-64g-ep8-b512{,-q,-t2}`, controls `/mwittmann/ncclep-64g-a2a-{ctl,b512}`.

Ranked next steps: (1) scope command-buffer disablement to the EP ops (both arms currently pay for global-off); (2) drop the redundant tail-zeroing pass; (3) MoE-layer chunking to unlock b1024+ (also NVIDIA's intended usage and the H-te chunked-pipeline shape); (4) `max_num_sms` sweep; (5) fp8 dispatch wire from the TE quantization WIP branch (ties into #7282).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-007: **MoE-layer chunking prototyped and derisked at the production config — b1024×seq4096 at 64 GPUs/EP8 now trains** (`/mwittmann/ncclep-64g-ep8-b1024-ck8k-r5`, 20 steps, first attempt):

| arm | batch | steady MFU (B200) | s/step | tok/s | final loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a2a_cute EP8 | 1024 | 19.1 % | 15.7 | 266 k | 8.7463 |
| **nccl_ep EP8, chunked C=8192** | 1024 | **18.0 %** | 16.6 | 252 k | **8.7450** |
| nccl_ep EP8, unchunked (prior) | 512 | 16.7–17.1 % | 8.9 | 233–240 k | 8.7598 |

The backend now splits each rank's token stream into fixed C-token chunks and `lax.scan`s dispatch → grouped FFN → combine per chunk, with **`jax.checkpoint` on the chunk body**. Both halves matter:

1. **Chunked dispatch** shrinks the TE staging + no-drop recv capacity to `ep × C × top_k` rows per dispatch (2.6 GiB at C=8192 vs 21.5 GiB monolithic).
2. **Chunk remat** is what actually clears the memory wall: without it, `scan` saves every chunk's capacity-sized tensors as backward residuals, and `K × (ep × C × top_k) = ep × T_local × top_k` — invariant of chunk size, i.e. the same ~165 GiB as the unchunked wall. A one-allocation discriminator job (a2a control PASS + three chunk sizes FAIL, one with an honest 164.93 GiB OOM) exposed this; with the checkpoint, backward recomputes one chunk at a time and peak EP memory is a single chunk's working set.

Consequence for scale derisk: **EP-side memory is now O(chunk), independent of batch and seqlen** — the "8k max_tokens_per_rank limits local batch" wall is fully gone on our side. Numerics are a pure token partition: step-0 loss bit-identical to unchunked; the loss edge over a2a_cute (8.745 vs 8.746) is consistent with no-drop vs cf-1.0 drops. Chunking costs nothing measurable in throughput (b1024-chunked 18.0 % ≥ b512-unchunked 17.1 %), leaving the same ~1 pp untuned gap to a2a_cute as before (command buffers globally off, redundant tail-zeroing, `max_num_sms` at auto, no chunk pipelining yet).

Remaining b1024-scale caveat, not nccl_ep-specific: the intermittent `cuModuleLoadData` CUBIN failure (B200MFU-036 — environmental, hits a2a/ring identically, no known flag mitigation) cost several retries tonight; the launcher now runs sequential in-job attempts with a shared compile cache (~10 min warm retries), and r5 passed on attempt 1.

Reproduction: `mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep-ncclep` @ 203858818 (`--ep-chunk-tokens`, chunk remat, retry loop, `experiments/ncclep/run_arms_b1024.sh` discriminator); full narrative in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md) (NCCLEP-007). Next candidates unchanged from the ranked list, now with chunking as the substrate for the real prize: pipelined chunks (dispatch k+1 overlapping FFN k), command-buffer scoping, fp8 wire (#7282).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-008/-009: **fairness correction + full TE MoE block benchmark.**

**Correction to the NCCLEP-006 framing** (raised in the #oa-nvidia thread): every `nccl_ep` arm so far used TE's NCCL_EP `ep_dispatch`/`ep_combine` primitives around **our own** QuACK/SonicMoE expert GEMMs and our own QB router. That was a controlled transport swap — valid for the transport question, but not a test of NVIDIA's recommended configuration, which is TE's whole fused MoE block (`transformer_engine.jax.moe.moe`, TE #2912 + #3116: fused sigmoid+top-k router → NCCL_EP dispatch → grouped-quantize + grouped GEMMs → NCCL_EP combine, one custom_vjp). The block merged into TE main 2026-07-10, seven days before our wheel build, so the stashed 68493d2 wheel already ships it — `moe.py` is byte-identical to today's main tip.

**NCCLEP-009: benchmarked the recommended path.** New `te_moe` backend (branch `mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep-ncclep` @ 81fcd979a) hands the entire MoE layer to `moe()`; grug's routing tensors feed only the observational stats and the QB bias update. Router parity: TE's sigmoid path (bias-steered top-k without gradient, sum-normalized weights × scaling factor 2.5) is our QB router up to the bias landing in score space instead of logit space — single-node smoke step-0 loss is bit-identical to the nccl_ep arms. Same wheel, same stock-jax 0.10.1 stack, three arms in ONE 16-node allocation (`/mwittmann/ncclep-b512-arms`), d5120 L48 e64 top4 seq4096 **b512** EP8, 64 GPUs, single copy data8×expert8, 20 steps; steady = median over steps ≥ 8:

| arm | steady MFU (B200 conv.) | s/step | tok/s | final loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a2a_cute EP8 (incumbent) | **18.28 %** | 8.21 | 256 k | 8.7617 |
| nccl_ep EP8 (TE transport + QuACK FFN) | 17.15 % | 8.75 | 240 k | 8.7598 |
| te_moe EP8 (full TE MoE block) | 16.94 % | 8.86 | 237 k | 8.7649 |

Takeaways:

1. **The full block ties the seam** (16.94 vs 17.15 %, within same-allocation step noise) — the "maybe our integration undersold NCCL_EP" hypothesis is answered. At this config the recommended path lands where our seam did, ~1.1–1.3 pp below a2a_cute, so the earlier conclusion survives the fairness correction, now with the recommended integration actually tested.
2. Corollary: our QuACK FFN ≈ TE's grouped GEMMs here (consistent with B200MFU-011) and the fused-router gain is negligible; the gap to a2a_cute sits in the EP transport/capacity structure, not expert compute.
3. Loss parity three ways; te_moe's +5e-3 final loss is consistent with the score-space bias placement.

Caveats that still favor a future TE arm: bf16 wire and bf16 grouped GEMMs only (fp8/MXFP8 quantizer sets are explicitly out of scope in today's `moe.py`, while NVIDIA's headline DeepSeek-v3 GB300 numbers ride the MXFP8 recipe); our wheel predates TE #3231 (EP dispatch/combine scheduled on XLA's collective stream, 2026-07-22) and #3226 (orthogonal-axes bootstrap — our replica-DP ask, 2026-07-23); stock jax rather than NGC JAX 26.05 (ragged-dot fusion, multi-stream collectives, host offloading); command buffers globally off in all three arms; `moe()` has no chunked-dispatch mode, so b1024 remains behind the no-drop capacity wall on the full block where our chunked seam trains at 18.0 % (NCCLEP-007).

Ranked next steps: (1) rebuild TE at main tip and rerun the TE arms (#3231 is a plausible real win); (2) fp8 wire + MXFP8 grouped quant when `moe.py` grows quantizer support (ties #7282); (3) an NGC JAX container arm to test the full deck stack; (4) upstream ask: chunked-dispatch mode in `moe()`.

Full narrative: [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md) (NCCLEP-008/-009).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 NCCLEP-010: **gap-closure benchmark — every non-quantization NVIDIA recommendation applied, in bf16.** Follow-up to NCCLEP-009's caveat list: TE rebuilt at main tip (#3231 EP-on-collective-stream, #3226), command-buffer capture scoped instead of globally off, multi-stream collective overlap (`--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=2`), an `ep_bootstrap max_num_sms` sweep, and the NGC 26.06 container arm. Two findings:

**1. TE main tip (ea41e08, 2026-07-24) is a regression on our topology.** Both TE integrations — the full `moe()` block and the bare `ep_dispatch`/`ep_combine` seam — deterministically die at first 64-GPU execution at data8×expert8 (`ncclCommSplit ... remote process exited`, gang-wide coordination-service SIGABRT; 2/2 attempts × 4 arms across two allocations; no CUBIN signature). 2-node (data1×expert8) and 4-node (data2×expert8) topologies pass, so the trigger needs the full subgroup-clique structure. An import-time shim stripping #3231's `compute_on("gpu_stream:collective")` pin does NOT fix it, which exonerates the stream annotation as sole cause and points at the NCCL_EP relocation to the new `3rdparty/nccl-extensions` submodule (2c6135a, a different nccl_ep code line than the in-tree `NVIDIA/nccl@b87848f` our 68493d2 wheel used). Worth raising in #oa-nvidia: this blocks validating exactly the EP-overlap work (#3231) NVIDIA shipped this week.

**2. On the wheel that trains (68493d2), every knob is a wash or a loss.** One 16-node allocation (`/mwittmann/ncclep-gapclose3-arms`), d5120 L48 e64 top4 seq4096 b512 EP8, steady = median over steps ≥ 8; a2a-tuned from the sibling allocation (`ncclep-gapclose-arms`, anchor 18.24 %):

| arm | steady MFU | s/step | final loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a2a_cute base | **18.24 %** | 8.23 | 8.7617 |
| a2a_cute tuned (default capture + overlap) | 18.19 % | 8.25 | 8.7616 |
| a2a_cute anchor (alloc 3) | 18.10 % | 8.29 | 8.7616 |
| nccl_ep seam + scoped capture + overlap | 17.15 % | 8.75 | 8.7598 |
| te_moe base | 16.82 % | 8.92 | 8.7649 |
| te_moe + scoped capture | 16.85 % | 8.90 | 8.7649 |
| te_moe + scoped capture + overlap | 16.78 % | 8.94 | 8.7649 |
| te_moe + … + max_num_sms 32 | 16.42 % | 9.13 | 8.7649 |
| te_moe + … + max_num_sms 16 | 15.73 % | 9.54 | 8.7649 |

Scoped capture (XLA default set minus CUSTOM_CALL) is safe with TE EP — settling the NCCLEP-006 "scope the command buffers" item — but is worth +0.03 pp; the overlap flag is ~−0.05 pp on both te_moe and a2a; `max_num_sms` is monotonically negative (auto > 32 > 16 — third falsification of SM budgeting on this stack after B200MFU-016/-021). The tuned seam reproduces its untuned 17.15 %. **The a2a_cute lead stands at ~1.3 pp over the best TE arm through every knob.** With quantization explicitly out of scope (fp8/MXFP8 wire not yet in `moe.py`), the remaining untested NVIDIA levers are the quantized block and the NGC stack.

NGC 26.06 status: the guarded-overlay machinery from #7421 works end-to-end for the bench (pinned wheel + per-sha JIT headers + patched PJRT plugin; 16×4 gang up, all ranks compiling), but the a2a_cute arm's `jit_train_step` compile under the NGC XLA has produced no output for >90 min (`/mwittmann/ngc-gc-a2a3`) — timeboxed and deferred along with the te_moe and ragged-dot-fusion-native NGC arms; will follow up.

Reproduction: branch `mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep-ncclep` @ 8664bb3c5 (`run_arms_gapclose{,2,3}.sh`, `launch_ngc.py`); tip-regression repro matrix in the [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7331-nccl-ep/.agents/logbooks/7331-nccl-ep.md) (NCCLEP-010). Ranked next: (1) report the tip regression + repro to NVIDIA (blocks #3231 validation); (2) quantized wire when `moe.py` grows it (#7282); (3) NGC arms once the compile stall is understood.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
*Request for comment.*

> **TL;DR.** OPD needs a teacher model that returns per-token logprob targets in the training inner
> loop. The deciding factor is **how many logprobs per token** we need: our stack (MarinSkyRL) today
> does **top-K sparse forward-KL** (default **K=256**), *not* the full-vocab reverse-KL of the
> DeepSeek-V4 recipe. Top-K payloads are small and travel cheaply over a network; **full-vocab is
> ~300 KB/token → GB/step and is only tractable co-located.** That single fact reorders the options.
>
> **My lean: Option 3 (permanent marin-serve teacher endpoints on CoreWeave, top-K), plus Option 4
> (forward-only co-located teacher) reserved as a "full-vocab fast-track" if an ablation ever shows
> we need it.** Option 3 reuses the remote teacher-client MarinSkyRL already has, decouples serving
> optimization from the RL loop, and amortizes across OPD + judge + eval. Options 1 and 2 are
> prototyping and single-hero-run tools, respectively. **Tell me where this is wrong** — especially
> on (a) whether K≤20 provider ceilings are disqualifying, (b) whether full-vocab reverse-KL is worth
> building for at all, and (c) whether the forward-only teacher (Option 4) should be the default
> instead of Option 3.

## Context

On-policy distillation (OPD) is load-bearing in our post-training plan: the distillation stage
distills RL-trained experts into the student via OPD, *if* we have teacher-logit infra — otherwise we
fall back to the weaker off-policy SFT-distill path. The [#7074](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7074)
cost analysis sizes the pipeline as **RL K experts → OPD into the student** (Nemotron-style path),
where the OPD leg is student-rollout-dominated and roughly RL-scale in cost.

**Why this decision matters NOW:** OPD is a complex, jointly-optimized system — the teacher serving
path is tightly coupled to the training loop (the teacher is queried in the inner loop, per batch of
student-generated tokens). Getting it working reliably is hard, and once it works there is a strong
incentive to never touch the plumbing again. That makes the early architectural choices effectively
*sticky*. This RFC aims to make that choice a deliberate one, with eyes open about what each option
forecloses.

The core question: **how do we serve the teacher model that provides logprob targets during OPD?**

---

## The logprobs crux (the deciding technical factor)

OPD's distillation loss is a per-token KL between the student and teacher distributions over the
generated positions. The teacher must return a **probability distribution over tokens** at each
position — not a generated sequence or a reward score. *How much* of that distribution we need is the
crux, and it splits cleanly into two regimes:

- **Top-K (what our stack does today).** MarinSkyRL's `distillation_trainer.py` requests
  `cfg.teacher.top_k_logprobs` (default **K=256**, `config/ppo_base_config.yaml`), carries a
  `teacher_top_k_logprobs: [batch, seq, K]` tensor (`training_batch.py`), and computes the loss with
  `forward_kl_from_sparse` (`utils/distillation_utils.py`) — a **forward**-KL over the teacher's
  top-K support (`kl = Σ_k teacher_p·(teacher_logp − student_logp_at_k)`). A remote
  `TeacherInferenceEngineClient.score_sequences` (with student↔teacher retokenization) already exists.
  **Top-K logprobs are a small payload** (K values + K indices per token) and travel cheaply over a
  network — so top-K OPD is *not* gated by where the teacher lives.
- **Full-vocab (the DeepSeek-V4 aspiration).** V4's OPD is full-vocabulary **reverse**-KL
  (`L = Σᵢ wᵢ·D_KL(π_θ ∥ π_Eᵢ)`, trajectories sampled from the student). This is a **different loss in
  both support (full vs top-K) and direction (reverse vs forward)** from what MarinSkyRL implements
  today. It is strictly richer — but per the bandwidth wrinkle below, it is only tractable with a
  **co-located** teacher.

**The bandwidth wrinkle (why top-K is the practical default, and why providers only offer top-k).**
A full-vocab logprob vector is ~vocab (≈128–150k) × 2 bytes ≈ **~300 KB per generated token**. Across
an OPD inner-loop batch that is **on the order of GB/step moving over the network, every step** — WAN
is prohibitive, intra-DC is heavy, and only a co-located teacher on the same NCCL/IPC fabric makes it
free. This is almost certainly *why* hosted providers expose only top-k logprobs (OpenAI: top-20): the
full distribution is too expensive to serialize per token. **Consequence:** any *networked* teacher —
a provider (Option 1) or a permanently hosted endpoint (Option 3) — is effectively **top-K only**.
Full-vocab reverse-KL is available only to a **co-located** teacher (Option 2's in-cluster engines, or
Option 4's forward-only teacher). If we want full-vocab, we want an **OPD fast-track for co-located
jobs** alongside whatever we run for the common case.

**Working assumption for this RFC:** unless an ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is worth its cost,
we should **plan for top-K** (start at the K our stack already defaults to, and treat provider K≤20 as
the one hard ceiling to check). Full-vocab is then an opt-in co-located path, not the baseline that
gates the whole serving decision. *(We found no published "safe K" ablation in our notes — see Q1.)*

---

## Option 1 — serve the teacher from a cloud inference provider (Together / Fireworks / OpenAI)

The teacher is a hosted model behind an API. The OPD trainer calls the provider's completions/chat
endpoint with `logprobs` to get per-token distributions.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Least new plumbing** — no serving infra to build or maintain; one less component to jointly optimize for throughput. | **Provider top-k ceiling vs. our K.** Providers cap logprobs low (OpenAI: top-20). Our stack defaults to **K=256**; whether K≤20 is adequate is an open ablation (Q1). Full-vocab reverse-KL is off the table on any provider. **This is the gating question for this option.** |
| **Maximum teacher flexibility** — swap teachers by changing a model name; no weight staging. | **Teacher availability is not in our control.** A provider can deprecate/drop a model mid-campaign; teacher selection follows their catalog, not our research needs. |
| **Fast to prototype** — an API key unblocks OPD-loop development today. | **No path to custom Marin teachers** — distilling from a Marin-trained checkpoint (the point of expert iteration) needs a separate deal / custom serving. |
| **Elastic capacity** — no fixed GPU commitment; pay per token. | **Per-token cost + throughput risk at scale.** OPD processes ~10⁹–10¹⁰ training tokens (#7074); provider pricing is expensive at that volume, and **rate-limit / tail-latency variance is an inner-loop hazard** — a single slow or throttled teacher call stalls the whole synchronous train step, not just a batch's cost. |
| | **Redundancy requires N integrations.** Each provider has a different API surface, logprob format, and rate-limit regime. Multi-provider fallback is real integration work, not a config flip. |
| | **Reproducibility risk** — providers may silently update served weights, breaking experiment reproducibility. |

---

## Option 2 — co-host the teacher with the student in a single large allocation

The teacher, student, and reference model all live in one Ray cluster / GPU allocation. The
teacher is a set of vLLM inference engines scheduled alongside the training actors. This is the
"everything in one Slurm job" model.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Infra already partially built** — MarinSkyRL already co-hosts policy + inference engines in one Ray cluster; the teacher is "one more served model," and the remote teacher-client already exists. | **The FLOP-utilization dance.** OPD is a 3-stage pipeline: student generates → teacher scores → student trains. When the student generates, the teacher is idle; when the teacher scores, the student is idle. Balancing all three at high utilization must be re-tuned per model size / batch / pipeline change. (SkyRL's `fully_async` 2-stage pipeline is already hard to balance; a 3rd stage compounds it.) |
| **Full control of quantization + weights** — quantized teachers, custom architectures, Marin-trained checkpoints all work. | **Resource-intensive** — a 120B-class teacher + student + reference in one allocation is a large footprint per experiment → **fewer concurrent experiments**. Trades experiment parallelism for self-contained runs. |
| **Low-latency hop** — teacher scoring is on the same Ray fabric as rollout, so batching is tight. | **Still top-K if the teacher is a vLLM engine** — vLLM's API returns top-K, not the full logits tensor (see Option 3 caveat). Full-vocab here needs a custom serving hook, i.e. it collapses into Option 4. |
| **Bugs are patchable** — full source access; no provider dependency. | **Infra burden** — one more thing the RL-launcher/SkyRL stack must schedule, configure, and debug. |

---

## Option 3 — permanently hosted teachers via marin-serve on dedicated CoreWeave compute

A set of CoreWeave GPUs is dedicated to long-running teacher endpoints (marin-serve / vLLM), queried
over the network by any consumer — OPD trainers, LLM judges, coding agents, eval pipelines, vibe
tests. The teacher is "always warm." **Top-K by nature of the network hop** (per the bandwidth crux).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Decoupled optimization** — the serving pipeline (continuous batching, prefix caching, quantization, KV-cache tuning) is optimized **independently** of the RL/OPD run. No joint-scheduling dance. | **Top-K only.** The network hop caps us at top-K logprobs (bandwidth crux) — fine for our current top-K forward-KL loss, but forecloses full-vocab reverse-KL. If the endpoint's K is enough (Q1), a non-issue; if we later want full-vocab, this option can't provide it (use Option 4). |
| **No top-*20* ceiling** — we run the model, so we set K (e.g. 256, matching our default) rather than being stuck at a provider's ~20. | **Resource-intensive** — dedicates GPUs full-time to hosting, removing them from the experiment pool. Trades raw training throughput for serving readiness. |
| **Multi-purpose amortization** — one hosted teacher serves OPD + the LLM-judge tier + coding agents + eval + vibe tests. The post-training plan already asks for "~10 hosted endpoints we can update quickly" — this *is* that infra, and concurrent OPD runs share it. | **High infra burden + single point of failure** — we own uptime, autoscaling, model-swapping, failure recovery. If the endpoint goes down, all dependent OPD runs stall. |
| **Marin-trained teachers work natively** — swap the hosted checkpoint; no provider deal, no API integration. Future-proof for expert-iteration. | **Forces teacher prioritization** — dedicated GPUs can't host every teacher at once; we commit to a small primary set, limiting experiment diversity. |
| **Faster wall-clock than Option 2** — continuous batching across all consumers + prefix caching means the teacher runs at high utilization *without* the pipeline-imbalance tax. | **Network latency** — same-region intra-DC RTT is sub-millisecond (negligible vs. WAN), but it is still a hop; per-batch latency is nonzero. |
| **Reuses existing plumbing** — MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` already targets a remote scoring engine and returns top-K; Option 3 is the closest to what's built. Also exercises marin-serve / the Inference Server ([#6500](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6500)) under real load. | |

---

## Option 4 — frozen, forward-only teacher co-resident in the trainer

A distinct implementation of "co-located": the teacher is a **frozen, forward-only** module in the
**training framework itself** (FSDP/Megatron forward pass, no generation engine), with the teacher
logits fed **straight into the loss**. This is a common OPD/KD setup and the only option that cleanly
supports **full-vocab reverse-KL**.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Full-vocab by construction, no serialization hop** — logits never leave the training mesh, so the ~300 KB/token bandwidth wall (and vLLM's top-K API limit) simply don't apply. The natural home for full-vocab reverse-KL. | **Teacher lives in the training allocation** — teacher weights occupy HBM in the same job; a 120B teacher + student + ref is a large single footprint (same experiment-parallelism cost as Option 2). |
| **No generation-serving stack to schedule** — no vLLM engine, no continuous-batching tuning, no separate endpoint. Just a forward pass, sharded like any frozen model. | **Teacher forward contends with training compute** on the same mesh; the forward FLOPs are inline with the step (though there's no idle-teacher pipeline-imbalance tax — the forward is a synchronous part of the loss). |
| **Simplest correctness story** — no cross-process logprob transport, no top-K renormalization approximation, no retokenization mismatch; teacher and student share the trainer's tokenizer/dtype. | **Least flexible swapping** — changing teachers means re-staging weights into the training job, not hitting a different endpoint. |
| **Exact reverse-KL** — student-sampled trajectories + full teacher distribution is precisely the V4 recipe. | **Not multi-purpose** — this teacher serves only the OPD loss and only for the run's duration; the "~10 hosted endpoints" need is unmet by this option (that's Option 3). |

---

## Cross-cutting considerations

### The teacher-oracle abstraction (delaying lock-in)

The core concern — early lock-in because OPD is hard to get working — applies to all four options. One
structural mitigation: **architect the OPD trainer against a generic `TeacherLogprobOracle` interface**
— given a batch of student-generated token sequences, return the teacher's logprob targets at each
position. The four options become four *backends* (API client, co-hosted vLLM, remote marin-serve
endpoint, in-trainer forward-only teacher). MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` is already
close to this boundary.

This makes the serving decision **reversible** for the *networked, top-K* backends (Options 1, 2-vLLM,
3 are interchangeable behind the interface). **The one seam the interface cannot paper over is top-K
vs full-vocab:** a full-vocab reverse-KL loss (Option 4) changes the loss's shape and the data the
oracle returns, so it is not a drop-in backend swap — it's a second loss path. Decide the
top-K-vs-full-vocab question first (Q1); *within* top-K, the backend is a swap.

### Quantization parity

For RL scoring, a quantized teacher (FP8/AWQ) is fine — the reward signal tolerates small logprob
perturbation. For **distillation**, the teacher's logprobs ARE the target, and quantization is a
systematic perturbation that compounds token-by-token. Options 2/3/4 give full control over teacher
quantization (and the ability to validate parity against an unquantized reference); Option 1's
quantization is whatever the provider serves. Whether it matters depends on teacher size and the loss's
error tolerance.

### The small-model distillation angle

The plan also ships smaller sizes via strong-to-weak distillation **from the flagship**. This is a
*different* OPD use case (flagship → small model, not expert → student) but reuses the same teacher
serving infra, and it is long-context / high-throughput / high-value. Whichever option we pick should
handle both.

---

## Open questions for discussion

1. **What K is safe? (the pivotal question)** Our stack defaults to **K=256** top-K forward-KL. Is
   K≤20 (provider ceiling, Option 1) adequate, or do we need K≈256 (self-hosted, Options 2/3), or true
   full-vocab reverse-KL (Option 4)? We found **no published safe-K ablation** in our notes — this
   likely needs a quick internal ablation, and its answer determines which options are even eligible.

2. **Is full-vocab reverse-KL worth building?** It's the DeepSeek-V4 recipe and strictly richer, but
   it's co-located-only (bandwidth) and a second loss path (not just a backend swap). If K=256 top-K
   forward-KL is "good enough," we can drop full-vocab entirely and the serving decision simplifies to
   Options 1/3. If not, Option 4 becomes load-bearing.

3. **Teacher size envelope:** What is the largest teacher we plan to distill from? A 120B-class teacher
   makes the co-located options (2/4) expensive (the allocation balloons) and pushes the common case
   toward Option 3. A ≤70B teacher is more tractable everywhere.

4. **Concurrency:** How many OPD experiments run simultaneously? "Many, sharing one teacher" → Option
   3's amortization dominates. "One at a time" → Option 2/4's self-contained simplicity is fine.

5. **Marin-trained teacher timeline:** When do we first need to distill from a Marin-trained checkpoint
   (not a third-party model)? That's the hard deadline by which Option 1 must be replaced by 2/3/4.

6. **Is a hybrid viable?** Option 3 (primary/production, top-K) + Option 1 as elastic overflow + Option
   4 as a full-vocab fast-track for the one hero run that needs it. The oracle abstraction makes the
   top-K backends interchangeable; Option 4 is the deliberate exception.

---

## Suggested framing for a decision

Rather than committing to one option now, a **phased path** that hedges lock-in:

1. **Phase 0 (fast):** Settle Q1 with a small **K ablation** (top-20 vs top-256 vs full-vocab on a
   representative teacher/student) — this is the decision that gates everything. In parallel, harden the
   `TeacherLogprobOracle` boundary around MarinSkyRL's existing top-K teacher-client, and validate the
   OPD loop end-to-end against **Option 1** (API, top-20) for loop correctness — the loop, not the
   backend, is the hard part.
2. **Phase 1:** Stand up a dedicated **marin-serve teacher endpoint (Option 3, top-K, K≈256)** for the
   primary production teacher; point the oracle at it. This is also the LLM-judge + eval endpoint the
   plan already needs, so the infra investment is shared, not OPD-specific.
3. **Phase 2 (conditional):** If — and only if — the Phase-0 ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is
   worth it, build **Option 4** (forward-only co-located teacher) as the full-vocab fast-track for the
   runs that need it. **Option 2** (co-hosted vLLM) is worth it only for a single large hero run where
   even Option 3's intra-DC hop is intolerable and full-vocab isn't required.

The interface boundary means the *top-K* backends are swaps, not redesigns. The genuinely sticky
decisions are the two the ablation forces: **top-K-vs-full-vocab** and **forward-vs-reverse KL**.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
Decisions here seem reasonable to me. Our experience so far has been that for trained models, the logprobs drop extremely quickly off of the top-few, so top-K feels pretty safe? Not sure the best way to validate that e.g. top-20/256/whatever wouldn't drop too much on the floor. I feel building things around the `TeacherLogprobOracle` interface is the right call - we can either present this via the OpenAI API against an inference provider or our own internal models, with little switching cost.

For running our own long-term inference endpoints, my concern would be two-fold: 

(a) yes, the maintainence burden, but that should be manageable, since we can run multiple instances and setup the clients to be failure tolerant. 
(b) GPUs are precious and we can't use the idled GPUs if they aren't being actively used by a trainer


For (b) if the server bringup is coupled to the data-gen/training process, I'm less concerned.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
This makes sense to me. Agree that it seems safer to start by co-scheduling the teacher and student, and only move to a more static teacher deployment if provably superior.

On thing not mentioned here: It seems to me that having some KV cache aware routing to inference workers might be really desirable here (independently of which option we pick).

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether increasing the MuonH MoE router z-loss from `1e-3` to `4e-3` improved the corrected MuonH matrix-swap variant at gate 1. The launcher ran the same model sizing, optimizer mask, data, schedule, output z-loss, and eval cadence as the parent ablation, changing only `router_z_loss_coef`. The two gate-1 runs finished successfully: at d512 the variant reached Paloma macro loss `3.7499`, slightly ahead of the corrected MuonH baseline `3.7542`, and at d768 it reached `3.3881`, ahead of `3.3988`. Effective speedup versus the v16 AdamH baseline was about `1.36x` at d512 and `1.34x` at d768; versus the corrected MuonH baseline it was about `1.02x` and `1.06x`. Conclusion: router z-loss `4e-3` passed gate 1 cleanly and looked especially useful at d768, with the next decision being whether to launch gate 2 at d1024 and d1280.

### Helpful links
- Gate-1 final results: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5600#issuecomment-4414574579
- W&B report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/MuonH-router-zloss-4e-3-vs-MuonH-vs-v16-AdamH-—-gate-1--VmlldzoxNjgyOTMwNg==
- Launcher PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5601
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Stacks on top of the corrected MuonH matrix-swap ablation (PR #5597, issue #5596) and tests whether raising `GrugModelConfig.router_z_loss_coef` from the README default of `1e-3` to `4e-3` improves the MuonH variant. Optimizer mask, model sizing, data, batch size, step count, schedule, output z-loss (`z_loss_weight=1e-4`), and eval cadence are unchanged.

Exact initiating prompts:

> how much z loss are applying?

> Let's launch a variant where we slightly increase router z-loss to 4e-3?

> Only launch it for muonh is enough

## Hypothesis or Goal

Under the MuonH matrix swap, tighter router-logit regularization (4× higher router z-loss) may stabilize routing and improve effective speedup at gate 1 (d512 at 2.19e17 FLOPs and d768 at 1.70e18 FLOPs) versus both the v16 AdamH baseline and the corrected MuonH baseline-adam-mask runs.

### Links

* Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe/muonh_router_zloss_sweep.py`
* Branch: `research/moe-muonh-router-zloss-4e-3` (stacked on `research/moe-muonh-matrix-sweep`)
* Parent MuonH ablation: #5596 / PR #5597
* Baseline reference: `experiments/grug/moe/README.md`

## Results

Not launched yet. Pre-commit and focused optimizer/contract tests pass on the new launcher; gate-1 build verified that `router_z_loss_coef` is overridden to `4e-3` on the resulting `GrugModelConfig`.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tests whether DPO on IFBench-style preference data improves instruction following without overfitting to IFBench or damaging IFEval. The first completed Tulu-3 8B DPO runs built the shared IFBench/IFEval evaluation path, trained strict/loose/soft preference arms, and found a real positive signal: all DPO arms improved IFBench_test strict pass-all over the Tulu base, with the loose arm best on IFBench (+9.33 percentage points strict), while IFEval stayed flat-to-up. The issue is still open because the stronger paper-style full-train strict dataset and LR sweep were launched next, but no later result has been recorded in the issue. Current recommendation: treat IFBench-targeted DPO as promising on Tulu, but do not conclude the full recipe until the full-coverage LR sweep results are added.

### Helpful links
- Initial Tulu DPO result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5244#issuecomment-2846928782
- W&B project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/ifbench_dpo
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

DPO against a narrow instruction-following spec may improve benchmark compliance while degrading broader instruction following. This project tracks whether IFBench-targeted DPO actually preserves or improves instruction-following behavior when evaluated on both IFEval and IFBench.

IFEval is the continuity baseline. IFBench is the primary target because it is the broader, more adversarial instruction-following benchmark for this work. We should compare base instruct models, external DPO models, and our DPO checkpoints under the same generation and scoring harness.

## Hypothesis or Goal

North star: improve IFBench and IFEval without creating a model that only overfits the IFBench verifier/spec.

Initial goals:

- Train DPO on preference pairs derived from IFBench-style pass/fail signals.
- Evaluate every candidate on both IFEval and IFBench with consistent chat templates, stop tokens, and generation config.
- Track whether DPO gains are isolated to IFBench or transfer to IFEval.
- Test whether mixing SFT data with DPO data regularizes the model toward general instruction following while retaining IFBench gains.

### Links

- Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/dpo_sft_codex.md`
- Shared project notes: `.agents/projects/dpo_sft.md`
- W&B project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/ifbench_dpo

## Results

Pending. Current runs include Tulu-3 8B DPO baselines and learning-rate sweeps on the paper-strict IFBench preference dataset.

comments.author: ahmeda14960
comments.body:
🤖 Update: initial Tülu DPO signal

- Built the eval path for the two target benchmarks: IFBench_test (300 OOD prompts) and Google IFEval (541 prompts), using the vendored IFBench/IFEvalG verifier stack and the shared scoring harness.
- Added and cached `allenai/Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-DPO` revision `a7beb67`, then used it as the base for Tülu-side DPO experiments.
- Trained three first-pass Tülu DPO arms over IFBench-derived preference data: `strict`, `loose`, and `soft`. The Tülu vocab/export mismatch was fixed with `resize_vocab_to_match_tokenizer=True`, and all three arms completed/exported.
- Evaluated Tülu base + DPO arms on both IFBench_test and IFEval. Early sign: DPO improves IFBench without obvious IFEval damage.

Key result:

```text
Model             IFBench strict   IFBench loose   IFEval strict   IFEval loose
Tülu base              20.00%          26.00%          76.52%         79.67%
+DPO strict            25.00%          28.67%          80.04%         82.44%
+DPO loose             29.33%          33.67%          78.93%         83.55%
+DPO soft              27.00%          30.67%          77.08%         80.78%
```

Initial read: the IFBench-targeted DPO signal is real on Tülu. All three DPO arms beat the base on IFBench_test strict pass-all; `loose` is the best OOD IFBench arm at +9.33pp strict over base. IFEval also stays flat-to-up, with `strict` best on IFEval strict and `loose` best on IFEval loose.

Current next step: we built the paper-style full-train strict dataset from Gemini-vs-Llama-8B rollouts, filtered to max length 4096 (`24,153` pairs), tokenized it region-agnostically in us-central1/east5, and launched a one-epoch Tülu LR sweep (`3e-6`, `5e-6`, `2e-5`) on v5p-8 in us-east5. These runs test whether the stronger full-coverage dataset can improve the IFBench lift while preserving IFEval.

It restores a hero checkpoint on one rack and autoregressively samples each prompt in its own batch row; `--step`/`--ckpt-dir` select the checkpoint (e.g. step-78000 from the wd/ragged-a2a tree), `--temperature`/`--seed`/`--max-new-tokens` control sampling, and prompts come from `--prompts-json` or `--prompts-file`. Results are written as JSON to the run's `analysis/` prefix.

            for i in range(2, num):
                if (num % i) == 0:
                    break
            else:
